summary:
Yucatán offers an administrative route to legal gender recognition. A 2024 reform to the state's Civil Registry Law, published in the Diario Oficial of 26 April 2024, created a procedure through which transgender people can update the legal gender on their identity documents without a court order. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state rundown of 11 March 2025 carries Yucatán on that basis, and the procedure is the fact a trans visitor's document situation turns on when entering or being stopped in the state.

Yucatán stands under Mexico's unfinished national framework for recognition. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure by that date and named six states whose legislatures had enacted none; Yucatán belongs to the 22. The same reporting warns that implementation differs sharply from one state to another, and that where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

Uneven implementation has concrete results. The Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) found that delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police. Those findings were set against killings including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

Analysis published by Caroline Beer on the LSE USAPP blog (22 November 2024) found that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so rights exist formally but are rarely enjoyed in practice. Beer stated explicitly that her earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ people in Mexico are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Trans-specific violence remains documented at scale. The Associated Press reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening period of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, which triggered LGBTQ+ outrage and street demonstrations. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that violence against trans people and the murder of LGBTI+ defenders had increased over the previous year. Transgender Europe monitoring recorded 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico from 2008 to September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a total second only to Brazil's 100.

Marriage equality in Yucatán is settled and has been for more than a decade. The Third District Court of the State of Yucatán ruled on 1 July 2013 that two petitioners were able to marry, and the first same-sex couple legally married in the state on 8 August 2013. The Yucatán Constitutional Court dismissed a challenge to the Civil Code's marriage provisions on 2 March 2015 and the federal Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 31 May 2015. The Congress of Yucatán passed a constitutional amendment allowing same-sex marriage on 7 September 2021 and amended secondary legislation to permit it on 1 March 2022.

Regional oversight bodies have pressed the authorities. In 2024 the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded investigation of all LGBTI violations using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may reach alarming levels.
tangentialFactors:
Legal protections elsewhere in Mexico set a higher floor than Yucatán's own record alone would suggest. Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide; it is named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished, and activists quoted at the time described the measure as critical to their feeling safe in the capital. No equivalent transfemicide statute is sourced for Yucatán.

Conversion-therapy bans are in force across a widening set of jurisdictions. Yucatán is listed as enacting a ban on 25 August 2021, alongside Mexico City's measure of 31 July 2020 and bans in other states. At national level the Chamber of Deputies passed a conversion-therapy ban in March 2023 by 267-104, following a 69-16 Senate vote in October 2022.

Same-sex acts have been decriminalised nationally since 1871, a baseline that has held across every state including Yucatán. Sexual diversity is documented as tolerated among Yucatán Maya groups, which distinguishes local social context from the statutory position without altering what the written law provides.
localsOnly:
Residents of Yucatán update legal gender through the state civil registry under the administrative procedure created by the 2024 Civil Registry Law reform, published in the Diario Oficial of 26 April 2024 on yucatan.gob.mx. Because the route is administrative rather than court-ordered, it does not require a judicial petition, unlike the recognition procedures that remain absent in six Mexican states.

State-level protections for residents were consolidated between 2021 and 2022: the Congress of Yucatán's constitutional amendment of 7 September 2021 and the secondary-legislation amendment of 1 March 2022 entrenched same-sex marriage, and the conversion-therapy ban enacted on 25 August 2021 constrains providers operating in the state.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not state processing times, required documents, fees, residency requirements or appeal routes for Yucatán's administrative recognition procedure; those conditions are unresolved on the present sourcing and would need to be checked against the Civil Registry Law text and civil-registry practice before travel.

Whether Yucatán's recognition procedure has been used consistently since 26 April 2024, and whether refusals or delays have been recorded there, is not sourced. Human Rights Watch's documented delays come from Tabasco, a different state, and cannot be assumed for Yucatán.

The named six states that had enacted no recognition procedure as of 31 March 2025 are not listed in the inventory, so their identity and any proximity to Yucatán remain unresolved.

Enforcement of Yucatán's conversion-therapy ban, and any prosecutions under it, are not sourced. Likewise no data is available here on hate-crime charging in Yucatán for offences motivated by gender identity.
